newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O.Licht - European beet sugar production 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: F.O.Licht - European beet sugar production 1997/98.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
FIRST ESTIMATE OF EUROPEAN BEET SUGAR PRODUCTION IN 1997/98
All figures in 1,000 tonnes, raw value, first figure 1997/98, second figure 1996/97.
Europe total 29913/30343
West Europe 21234/20672
East Europe 8679/9671

Austria 482/535, Belgium-Luxembourg 1100/1036, Denmark 560/547, Finland 170/150, France 4840/4572, Germany 4330/4570, Greece 396/288, Ireland 265/247, Italy 1785/1561, Netherlands 1196/1125, Portugal 27/2, Spain 1228/1307, Sweden 435/432, UK 1700/1609, EU total 18514/17981.

Switzerland 179/203, Turkey 2135/2024, ex Yugoslavia 406/464, West Europe total 21234/20672, Czech Republic 533/663, Slovakia 247/246, Hungary 475/613, Poland 1956/2496, Russia 1795/1870, Ukraine 2900/2935, East Europe total 8679/9671.

World sugar stocks may well come down in 1997/98. But it is most unlikely to be on account of a significant fall in output in Europe. Beet sugar production in the EU is now estimated at 18.5 million tonnes, in raw value terms, somewhat more than was produced the previous year while the figure for Western Europe in total is currently expected to reach 21.2 million tonnes or 27 per cent more as was produced the previous year.

Output in Eastern Europe is now put at 8.7 million tonnes. This is not only some way below what we had forecast in our mid-July assessment but is also below the total attained last season. Taking the two sectors together European beet sugar output is now put at 29.9 million tonnes, which is roughly 400,000 tonnes lower than was reached in 1996/97.

Quite diverse conditions have been experienced in Europe this season but it is not only the weather but political decisions which have influenced crop outlooks. Climatic conditions have been excellent in France, the largest producer in the EU, which seems to be heading for a record crop.

Conditions have not been the same in Germany, the second largest producer in the EU. The plant density is greater but the area is slightly down. Meanwhile early beet tests are less promising than last year's.
In the UK beet and sugar weight were excellent last season; this year tests suggest they will be better so an even higher crop is on the cards.
Turkey appears to have overcome the difficulties of the past few years and the country will become an exporter again this year. The industry plans to export 200,000 tonnes of white sugar during 1997.

Varied conditions prevail in East Europe. One of the problems with forecasting in respect of many countries in this region is the practice of setting targets which then become the accepted figures until they are proved wrong. In Russia, despite a reduced area, a beet harvest of 22 million tonnes has been set for 1997 compared with last season's 16 million tonnes.

The crop is in a better state so sugar output may reach about last season's figure. The Russian government has approved a plan to increase the output of sugar to 4 million tonnes, white value, by the year 2005; that would be an increase of more than 100 per cent, which raises some doubts about the target being reached.

Taxes imposed by Russia on imports of Ukrainian sugar have dealt a severe blow to that country's sugar industry. High production costs mean that if surplus sugar cannot be sold to Russia it is difficult to see where else it might go. Consequently the area has been reduced by more than 20 per cent. Last season the crop suffered from a protracted drought so sugar output may not be down on last season.

Polish farms and villages have suffered grievous harm from recent floods but it appears that little long term damage has been sustained by the sugar industry. A record crop last year which was well in excess of domestic needs led to serious financial problems as production costs are well in excess of what may be recouped from the world market.
The area this season has been reduced from 451,000 ha to 408,000 ha but sugar output is still expected to top the two million tonnes mark which will once again be in excess of national needs.

The changes in European output and possible reduction compared with 1996/97 are unlikely to have much impact on world market prices. However, taken in combination with likely falls in output in other parts of the world, a limited reduction in world stocks may be possible.

A cursory glance at the production figures for 1997/98 reveals that world sugar production in September/August could be around 123 million tonnes down from the 123.7 million tonnes produced the previous year. Consumption is expected to grow by more than 2 million tonnes, which taking into consideration unrecorded consumption, could reduce stocks by more than 1.5 million tonnes.

Surplus stocks are also projected to fall noticeably mainly in India, which could force the country to once again change its status from net exporter to net importer. Hence the fundamental situation in 1997/98 could develop favourably which should provide some underlying support.
